(1) The political guidelines for the European Commission’s 2024-2029 term3, sets out a plan for the Union’s sustainable prosperity and competitiveness. Making business easier and deepening the Single Market are among the key priorities while staying the course on Union´s climate and environmental goals.

---

3 Europe’s Choice, Political Guidelines for the next European Commission 2024−2029, Ursula von der Leyen / (2) The Union has committed to the accelerated decarbonisation of its economy to achieve climate neutrality, namely net-zero emissions or emissions after the deduction of removals, by 2050. That objective is at the heart of the European Green Deal and is in line with the Union’s commitment to global climate action under the Paris Agreement and should be achieved with respect to the goals of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. / (3) At the same time, the findings of the 2024 Draghi report4 indicate that lengthy and uncertain permit granting procedures are an obstacle for the roll-out of critical projects such as new power supply and grids. The Clean Industrial Deal Communication5 indicates that it is to speed up permit granting procedures, in particular for the deployment of grids, energy storage and renewables projects, industrial access to energy and industrial decarbonisation projects as well as manufacturing of clean technologies. Faster permit granting procedures are necessary, amongst others, for EuroHPC supercomputer facilities and semiconductor projects. Also, this is needed for projects supporting the digital transition, for those related to the decarbonisation of maritime and inland ports, airports and railways of trans-European transport network. Faster permitting is also necessary for projects which are critical to ensure food security in the Union.

---

4 Draghi, M. (2024) The future of European competitiveness. Available at: The Draghi report on EU competitiveness 5 Communication from the Commission to the European Parliament, the Council, The EUROPEAN Economic and Social Committee and the Committee of the Regions of 26 February 2025, The Clean Industrial Deal: A joint roadmap for competitiveness and decarbonisation (COM(2025) 85 final). / deleted / (4a) In order to reduce unnecessary administrative burden for project developers while ensuring a high level of protection of the environment, Member States should provide transparent and predictable assistance throughout environmental assessment procedures. To that end, they should publish and regularly update guidance as regards the scope and level of detail of the information required from project developers for different categories of projects and situations, in line with Commission guidance on screening and environmental impact assessment requirements under Directive 2011/92/EU. In addition, in the context of joint or coordinated procedures and in line with the ‘once-only principle’, developers should not be required to submit the same information or documents more than once where those have already been submitted to the competent authorities involved. This should be without prejudice to requests for updates, clarifications or additional information necessary for the assessment of the application concerned. / (5) Procedures linked to environmental assessments should be accelerated and streamlined for plans, programmes and projects across all sectors of the economy by securing qualified staff, expertise and resources in competent authorities, avoiding any overlap or unnecessary administrative burdens and establishing a common acceleration framework for environmental assessments in order to boost Union’s roll out of key technologies, reduce dependencies and strengthen competitiveness.
